Volume Estimation — Think Before You Count
Fraction Builder — Parts of a Whole
Base 10 Place Value — Building Numbers in 3D
Volume Fluency Maze — Measure to Navigate
Geometry Harbor - An Area and Volume Expedition

activities.title: One layer becomes a solid
activities.challenge: Examine the blue prism. Predict how many cubes are in one layer and how many are in all three layers, then use Measure on the model to compare your prediction.
activities.hint: The base is 6 by 4, so one layer covers 24 square units. There are 3 identical layers: 24 × 3. Measure selects the whole connected model, not just its top layer.
successCriteria: I distinguish a base area of 24 square units from a volume of 72 cubic units.
I can explain why multiplying by 3 counts every layer once.
activities.reflection: Why does area use square units while the complete model uses cubic units?

activities.title: Same volume, different silhouette
activities.challenge: Compare the tall gold prism with the lower blue prism across the aisle. Predict which contains more cubes, then measure each model and explain the result.
activities.hint: Gold has 9 square units in each of 8 layers. Blue has 24 in each of 3 layers. Both products are 72 even though their heights and footprints differ.
successCriteria: I measured 72 cubic units in each model.
I can explain how a smaller base and a greater height can preserve volume.
activities.reflection: Which model would fit better on a narrow shelf, and what other dimension would you need to check?

activities.title: Read the striped layers
activities.challenge: Walk around the striped prism and count its four layers. Predict its occupied volume and how many cubes use each material before measuring.
activities.hint: Each layer contains 5 × 5 = 25 cubes. Two sand layers contribute 50 cubes and two wood layers contribute another 50. Touching colors are measured together.
successCriteria: I distinguish four physical layers from two material types, with 50 cubes of each.
activities.reflection: If you added a fifth layer, what would change about the volume and the model’s height?

activities.title: Count every outside face
activities.challenge: Compare the full exposed surface areas of the blue and gold prisms. Include all six sides, including the underside, as if each model were lifted off the ground. Measure each model to check your totals.
activities.hint: A rectangular prism has three pairs of faces. Blue: 2 × (6×4 + 6×3 + 4×3) = 108 square units. Gold: 2 × (3×3 + 3×8 + 3×8) = 114. The separate ground is not part of either measured model.
successCriteria: I counted all six sides and found 108 square units for blue and 114 for gold.
I explain why two 72-unit volumes can need different amounts of covering material.
activities.reflection: Which model needs less wrapping, and how much less? Would the answer change if the underside did not need covering?

activities.title: Make your own layered prism
activities.challenge: Build a 24-cubic-unit prism from full cubes on the empty sand pad. Explain its base area and number of layers. If you want another challenge, build a different 24-unit prism beside it with an empty gap.
activities.hint: Try a 4 by 3 base and 2 layers: 12 × 2 = 24. A 3 by 2 base with 4 layers also works. Keep separate examples apart so Measure can select each connected build independently.
successCriteria: My own connected build measures 24 cubic units.
I recorded its base area, height and an explanation of why their product is 24.
activities.reflection: What did changing the base and height do to your model’s silhouette? Review your evidence here; this build is a self-review activity, not an automatically scored task.
